svg.title: MVP versus finished architecture, side by side
svg.desc: The MVP is a focused four-screen pipeline: search, planner, cart, profile. The finished architecture wraps the same pipeline in intent routing, generators, trust and arbitration, and persistent personalization, without more screens.
svg.text: Architectural growth, not just feature count — more capability without more screens

g.text: Mobile (4 tabs) → Backend → Search → 9 Adapters
● Product search + live multi-store price compare
● Smart Planner: multi-item list, brute-force route/store optimization
● Cart with per-store subtotals, trip-time estimate
● Guest-first: ZIP code is the only thing required
● No AI, no LLM calls, no personalization
• Smaller surface area, easier to test end to end
• Fewer failure points across 9 already-flaky retailer sources
• Predictable UX — nothing an LLM might improvise
• Faster path to App Store review
• Lower operational cost — one process, in-memory cache

svg.text: Fridge · Meal Planner · Assistant · Product Quality Scan
Barcode Scan · List OCR · Voice Entry · Savings · Advisor Insights
code exists on disk, no navigation entry point wired up

g.text: + Intent Router → Generators → Trust/Arbitration → 3 shapes
● Same search/compare/planner core, untouched underneath
● Voice + camera as second Perception paths into one router
● Meal planning, nutrition gap analysis, food-waste nudges
● Budget as a shared constraint object, not a dashboard
● One ranked-suggestion queue instead of per-feature nagging

svg.text: What it costs to get there

g.text: • Real infrastructure: LLM calls, rate limits, vision boundary
• A trust layer that can say no — or nothing surfaces at all
• Account-backed persistence, not just AsyncStorage
• More failure modes to design honest fallbacks for
• Harder to test: nine generators, one shared arbitration layer

svg.text: A good MVP isn't a smaller final product —
it's the architecture that validates the core
assumption with the least unnecessary complexity.
